Although much remains to be learned about many species, particularly non-game species, management of wild populations has reached a high degree of skill in this country. Proper use of this knowledge and use of research to answer our unknowns should bring about recovery of many species. Frank appraisal of the health of some endangered populations tells us not all our efforts will be successful. Nevertheless, considerable positive impacts on endangered animals will occur.
Benefits to native U.S. species will occur in three ways:
1. Under the proposed legislation, it will be possible for the Secretary to list a species as endangered under Group 2 to help prevent actions which could adversly affect it. Isolated populations are vulnerable even at normal distribution and numbers. As soon as a threat appears the population may be classed as endangered. If the threat is diverted before the population or habitat is changed, there will not be an impact on the species.
2. With similar isolated populations which have been severely reduced, successful restoration certainly will bring about a considerable positive impact on the endangered species and probably associated species as well. But the impact, as important as it is to the endangered species, is limited in scope. The Puerto Rican parrot population is down to where there are no more than 14 or 15 birds in the wild.
